video.titulo: Why Spain Stayed Out of WW2 #history #didyouknow #ww2

transcricao:
During World War II, all of Europe was tearing itself apart. So, why was Spain the one country that managed to stay out of it? It wasn't that Spain didn't want to fight, it was that Spain simply couldn't afford to. 1939, Spain had just come out of a 3-year civil war that killed 500,000 people and left the entire country in ruins.

Factories had shut down, agriculture had collapsed, the military was exhausted, and the whole of society was on the verge of falling apart. At that point, Spain not descending into chaos again was already a miracle, let alone launching a war against anyone else. So, not long after World War II broke out, >> >> Spain declared neutrality. On May 10th, 1940, Germany launched Case Yellow on the Western Front, unleashing a blitzkrieg on France and the Low Countries.

The French defensive line collapsed almost immediately, shocking the entire world, and it sparked Franco's ambitions. He hastened to write a letter to Hitler to express Spain's desire to join the war, but Hitler didn't take the letter seriously at all. He figured Britain wouldn't last much longer anyway. He didn't need Spain sticking its nose in.

What he didn't expect was that just a few months later, Operation Sealion stalled. Hitler realized Britain was a much tougher opponent than he'd thought, and shifted to a broader strategy of driving Britain out of the Mediterranean. The key to that plan was capturing Gibraltar. So, Hitler went back to Franco.

>> Spain joins us. We take Gibraltar. We need weapons, food, Morocco, the Canary Islands, Spanish Guinea, Equatorial, and the western half of Algeria, and a written apology from France, and a pony. I would rather have three or four teeth pulled than go through that again.

>> The two men talked for 7 hours and parted ways with nothing resolved. Even though Spain never joined the Axis, that didn't mean it wasn't helping Germany. After the Soviet-German war broke out in 1941, Franco used anti-communism as a banner and recruited around 18,000 Spanish volunteers, forming them into the Blue Division, which fought alongside German forces in the invasion of the Soviet Union. By 1942, the tide had turned.

Germany was crushed at Stalingrad, and the Allies had landed North Africa. Franco realized the Axis defeat was now inevitable, so he quietly began shifting toward the Allies, pulling the Blue Division back, stopping the export of strategic resources to Germany, and making sure he had a way out.
